name: Cholesterol ratio
seoDesc: Cholesterol ratio: work out HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein from the total cholesterol and the cholesterol / HDL ratio. A free health calculator with the…
summary: Supply the total cholesterol, the cholesterol / HDL ratio and the LDL / HDL ratio and the Cholesterol ratio calculator solves for HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Press Calculate for the answer; change a value and it steps off screen until you press again, so each edit can be judged on its own.

sections.title: How does the Cholesterol ratio calculator work?
sections.html:
The Cholesterol ratio calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the total cholesterol, the cholesterol / HDL ratio and the LDL / HDL ratio.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in milligrams per deciliter. The unit chip switches it to any of the 2 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show the above ratio in mmol/L”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Cholesterol ratio calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein=total cholesterol ÷ cholesterol ÷ HDL ratio
LDL — Low-Density Lipoprotein=HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein × LDL ÷ HDL ratio
HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein=TG − Triglycerides ÷ triglycerides ÷ HDL ratio
HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein=(2183 ÷ 5000) × TG − Triglycerides ÷ triglycerides ÷ HDL ratio
TG - Triglycerides=-5 × HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein − 5 × LDL — Low-Density Lipoprotein + 5 × total cholesterol

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Total cholesterol = 10 Mg/d l and Cholesterol / HDL ratio = 10. Working through the relationship above gives HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein = 1 Mg/d l.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein = 1 Mg/d l should be roughly the size you expected from Total cholesterol = 10 Mg/d l and Cholesterol / HDL ratio = 10.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for HDL or LDL, opening in milligrams per deciliter
  • Cholesterol – for triglycerides, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Cholesterol ratio calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total cholesterol, the cholesterol / HDL ratio and the LDL / HDL ratio — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Cholesterol ratio calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein, derived from the total cholesterol, the cholesterol / HDL ratio and the LDL / HDL ratio. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Cholesterol ratio calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total cholesterol, the cholesterol / HDL ratio and the LDL / HDL ratio, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total cholesterol in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total cholesterol opens in milligrams per deciliter and the chip beside it offers 2 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports HDL — High-Density Lipoprotein = 1 Mg/d l. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Cholesterol ratio calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
